title: ADME II: Metabolism & Excretion Overview
summary: Where drugs go to be cleared and how structure steers that.

lessons.title: Clearance concepts for chemists

levels.kid:
Your body is always cleaning up. Medicine that goes in has to come out again, or it would pile up forever.

**Clearance** is how fast the body cleans medicine out of the blood. Think of a bathtub with the drain open. If the drain is big, the water leaves fast. If the drain is tiny, the water stays a long time.

Two big drains clean medicine: the **liver**, which breaks medicine into new pieces, and the **kidneys**, which wash it out in pee. Chemists change the shape of a medicine so the drain works at just the right speed: not so fast that the medicine is gone too soon, and not so slow that it builds up.
levels.hs:
**Clearance (CL)** describes how efficiently the body removes a drug from the blood. Formally, it is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time, so its units are volume per time (for example mL/min or L/h). It is not the amount removed; it is a measure of the "cleaning power" of the organs.

The total clearance is the sum of the organs doing the work: **hepatic** clearance (the liver metabolizing the drug), **renal** clearance (the kidneys excreting it) and smaller routes such as bile or lungs.

Clearance matters because it sets how much drug stays in the body over time. A drug with high clearance disappears quickly and may need frequent dosing or a different design. A drug with very low clearance can accumulate.

Clearance works together with the **volume of distribution (Vd)** to set the **half-life**: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL. So a long half-life can come from low clearance, a large volume, or both.

Medicinal chemists measure clearance early, often in liver cells in a dish, and tweak the structure to bring it into a useful range.
levels.college:
**Definition.** Clearance is the proportionality constant between elimination rate and plasma concentration: rate of elimination = CL × C. Because exposure after a dose is AUC = F × Dose / CL, clearance is the main structural lever on exposure, while Vd mainly governs half-life together with CL (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL).

**Additivity.** Total CL = CLH + CLR + CLother. Each organ's clearance cannot exceed its blood flow: hepatic blood flow is roughly 1.5 L/min in an adult, so blood clearance above that implies extrahepatic metabolism.

**Hepatic clearance and the well-stirred model.** CLH = QH × fu × CLint / (QH + fu × CLint), where fu is the unbound fraction in blood and CLint the intrinsic metabolic capacity of the liver.
- **Low-extraction drugs** (EH below about 0.3): CLH ≈ fu × CLint. Clearance is sensitive to enzyme inhibition, induction and changes in protein binding.
- **High-extraction drugs** (EH above about 0.7): CLH ≈ QH. Clearance is flow-limited; oral bioavailability is low because of first pass.

**Renal clearance.** CLR = fu × GFR when the drug is only filtered; values above fu × GFR imply net tubular secretion, below imply reabsorption.

**Why chemists care.** Lipophilic, neutral compounds tend to be cleared by metabolism; polar, low-logD compounds are often cleared unchanged by the kidney. Lowering logD usually lowers CLint, a reliable first move when metabolic clearance is too high.
levels.phd:
**Unbound clearance as the real target.** Because only unbound drug is generally available to enzymes and transporters, the medicinal chemist's design variable is unbound intrinsic clearance (CLint,u). Total clearance can mislead: raising plasma protein binding lowers total CL for a low-extraction drug, but unbound exposure (AUCu = F × Dose / CLint,u for an oral low-extraction drug) is unchanged. This is why "improving" half-life by adding albumin binding often buys nothing pharmacologically, a point argued forcefully by Smith, Di and Kerns.

**Liver models.** The well-stirred model is most used; the parallel-tube and dispersion models predict higher clearance for high-CLint compounds. Differences matter mainly at high extraction. All assume perfusion-limited uptake. For OATP substrates (many acids, statins), the **extended clearance model** applies: CLH depends on active uptake (PSinf), passive diffusion, metabolism and biliary efflux, and hepatic uptake can be rate-determining, so microsomal CLint underpredicts.

**Half-life is a dependent variable.** t½ depends on both CL and Vd. Lipophilic bases often have long half-lives from large Vd (tissue phospholipid binding), not low clearance. Structural changes that lower logD may lower CL and Vd together, leaving t½ unchanged: a classic frustration.

**Extrapolation (IVIVE).** CLint from microsomes or hepatocytes is scaled by physiological factors (microsomal protein or hepatocytes per gram liver, liver weight per body weight) and corrected for nonspecific incubation binding (fu,inc). Systematic underprediction, often several-fold, is common, especially for low-turnover and transporter-dependent compounds; empirical regression corrections are widespread.

**Allometry and species.** Rat, dog and monkey clearance scale to human with exponents near 0.75, but metabolism by species-specific enzymes (aldehyde oxidase, certain CYPs) breaks simple allometry.
levels.expert:
**How a project team uses clearance.** The question is never "is clearance low?" but "is unbound exposure at the target adequate for a practical regimen, with acceptable variability and interaction risk?" Teams set a target product profile early (for example, once-daily oral, dose that is formulable) and back-calculate the CLint,u and Vd needed.

**Practical heuristics.**
- Measure fu and fu,inc before arguing about CL; many "low-clearance improvements" are binding artefacts.
- Check whether clearance is metabolic, renal or biliary before redesigning. In rats, a cannulated bile duct study or urine collection quickly tells you where the drug is going.
- If in vivo CL exceeds hepatic blood flow, look for blood instability, extrahepatic metabolism or high blood-to-plasma partitioning.
- Low-extraction compounds cleared by a single CYP (especially CYP3A4) carry interaction risk; aim for balanced clearance routes.

**Pitfalls seasoned DMPK scientists watch for.**
- Microsomes miss non-CYP pathways: aldehyde oxidase (cytosolic), UGTs without pore-forming agents, esterases, and transporter-limited uptake. Hepatocytes are the safer screen.
- Aldehyde oxidase activity is high in humans and monkeys but much lower in dogs and rats, so azaheterocycles that look stable preclinically can clear rapidly in humans.
- Renal clearance does not scale like metabolism; a polar zwitterion cleared by OAT secretion may behave differently in humans.

**Clinical tie-in.** Hepatic impairment hits high-extraction drugs through reduced flow and portosystemic shunting, low-extraction drugs through lost CLint and altered binding. Renal impairment matters when renal clearance is a large share of total; this is why labels often carry adjustment guidance based on estimated kidney function, and why a dual-cleared molecule is valued: it degrades gracefully when one organ fails.

keyPoints: Clearance = elimination rate ÷ plasma concentration; units of volume per time.
Total CL = hepatic + renal + other routes; AUC = F × Dose / CL.
t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL: half-life depends on both clearance and volume.
Low-extraction drugs: CL ≈ fu × CLint; high-extraction drugs: CL ≈ hepatic blood flow.
Lowering logD usually lowers metabolic intrinsic clearance.

lessons.title: First-pass metabolism

levels.kid:
When you swallow a pill, the medicine does not go straight to the rest of your body. First it goes from your tummy to your **liver**.

The liver is like a guard at a castle gate. It checks everything coming from the tummy and breaks some medicine apart before it can get through. This is called **first-pass**, because it happens on the medicine's first trip.

For some medicines, the guard breaks almost all of it! So doctors give those medicines a different way, like **under the tongue** or as a **shot**, to sneak around the gate. Chemists can also change a medicine's shape so the guard doesn't grab it so easily.
levels.hs:
**First-pass metabolism** is the loss of drug before it reaches the general (systemic) circulation after you swallow it.

Here is the path. A swallowed drug is absorbed through the wall of the small intestine. Blood from the gut does not go straight to the heart; it drains into the **hepatic portal vein**, which goes to the **liver**. Both the gut wall and the liver contain enzymes (especially the **CYP450** family) that can metabolize the drug on this first pass.

The result is lower **oral bioavailability (F)**, the fraction of the dose that reaches the blood unchanged.

Examples:
- **Nitroglycerin** has very high first-pass loss, so it is given under the tongue (sublingual) for chest pain; those veins skip the liver.
- **Lidocaine** is not given as a pill for heart rhythm problems because the liver removes too much.
- **Propranolol** works orally, but much of each dose is lost to first pass.

Ways around first pass include other routes (sublingual, skin patches, inhaled, injection), prodrugs, and redesigning the molecule so the enzymes metabolize it more slowly.
levels.college:
**Components.** Oral bioavailability F = fa × fg × fh, where fg is the fraction escaping gut-wall metabolism and fh = 1 − EH the fraction escaping hepatic extraction. First pass describes the losses captured by fg and fh.

**Gut wall.** Enterocytes of the upper small intestine express CYP3A4, UGTs and SULTs, plus the efflux transporter P-gp. P-gp repeatedly pumps substrates back into the lumen, increasing their exposure to enterocyte CYP3A4, a cooperative "recycling" effect. Midazolam, cyclosporine, felodipine and simvastatin all show substantial gut extraction. Grapefruit furanocoumarins inactivate intestinal (not hepatic) CYP3A4, raising oral but not IV exposure.

**Liver.** For a drug cleared mainly by the liver, EH ≈ CLH / QH (blood). High-clearance drugs (EH above about 0.7) such as propranolol, verapamil and lidocaine have low oral F despite complete absorption.

**Consequences.**
- Large between-patient variability in oral exposure, since enzyme expression and blood flow vary.
- Oral doses much larger than IV doses for the same effect.
- Metabolites may form in high amounts after oral but not IV dosing, sometimes active or toxic.

**Bypass routes.** Sublingual and buccal drainage enters the superior vena cava system. Transdermal, inhaled, IV, IM and SC routes avoid portal delivery. Rectal dosing partly avoids it, because lower rectal veins drain systemically while the superior rectal vein drains to the portal system.

**Chemical strategies.** Reduce CYP3A4 affinity (lower logD, fewer soft spots), block metabolically labile positions, or use prodrugs that reach the systemic circulation before activation.
levels.phd:
**Quantifying the pieces.** Separating fa, fg and fh requires IV and oral data plus a measure of hepatic extraction: fh is estimated from IV blood clearance (fh = 1 − CLH,b/QH), and fa × fg is obtained as F/fh. Distinguishing fa from fg further needs permeability data or portal vein sampling in animals. The **Qgut model** (Yang, Rostami-Hodjegan and colleagues) predicts fg from enterocytic CLint and a hybrid flow term that combines villous blood flow and permeability: fg = Qgut / (Qgut + fu,gut × CLint,gut).

**Transporter–enzyme interplay.** Benet's hypothesis that P-gp increases intestinal CYP3A4 extraction by prolonging enterocyte residence is supported by sirolimus and tacrolimus data but its quantitative importance is debated. BDDCS (Wu and Benet) predicts that transporter effects on oral absorption dominate for class 3 and 4 (low-metabolism) compounds, while efflux–enzyme interplay matters most for class 2 (high-permeability, low-solubility, extensively metabolized) drugs.

**Saturable first pass.** For some drugs first-pass enzymes saturate at high luminal concentrations, giving greater-than-proportional increases in exposure with dose (nonlinear PK). Formulation (dissolution rate) can therefore change F, not just Tmax.

**Lymphatic route.** Highly lipophilic compounds (logP above about 5, with good triglyceride solubility) may enter chylomicrons and reach the systemic circulation through the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver; oral testosterone undecanoate exploits this.

**Deuteration.** Replacing C–H with C–D at the rate-limiting site slows CYP-mediated cleavage through a primary kinetic isotope effect, but only if C–H cleavage is rate-limiting and metabolic switching does not occur. Deutetrabenazine is a deuterated analog of tetrabenazine; deuterating its methoxy groups slows CYP2D6-mediated O-demethylation of its active metabolites, changing their pharmacokinetics.
levels.expert:
**Reading the data like a DMPK lead.** Low oral F has several causes, and fixing the wrong one wastes months. Before redesigning for metabolism, check:
- **Solubility and dissolution**: does F rise with a solution formulation? Then the problem is fa.
- **Permeability and efflux**: Caco-2 or MDCK-MDR1 efflux ratio, plus rat studies with a P-gp inhibitor.
- **Hepatic extraction**: is IV blood clearance near hepatic blood flow? Then fh is low and only clearance reduction will help.
- **Gut extraction**: a compound with modest hepatic clearance but low F and high CYP3A4 turnover suggests fg.

**Species traps.** Rat and dog gut CYP content and activity differ from human; monkey intestinal metabolism is often higher than human, so monkey F may underestimate human F for CYP3A substrates. Rat F usually underpredicts poorly-soluble compound performance in humans because of differing GI physiology.

**Clinical consequences to anticipate.**
- **Interactions**: drugs with high first-pass CYP3A4 loss are most vulnerable to strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (large exposure rises) and inducers (exposure collapse). Labels for such drugs often contraindicate combination with strong inhibitors.
- **Liver disease**: portosystemic shunting in cirrhosis can multiply oral exposure of high-extraction drugs while IV exposure changes less.
- **Food**: food can increase hepatic blood flow and transiently reduce first-pass extraction for some high-extraction drugs, raising F.

**Design choices.** Prodrugs activated in plasma rather than in the liver, sublingual or transdermal products for potent, lipophilic, low-molecular-weight agents, and soft spot blocking are the standard tools. Teams should also ask whether first-pass metabolites contribute activity or toxicity, since oral and IV metabolite ratios can differ dramatically.

keyPoints: First pass = drug lost in gut wall and liver before reaching systemic circulation.
Gut blood drains via the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
Oral F = fa × fg × fh; first pass lowers fg and fh.
Sublingual, transdermal, inhaled and injected routes bypass portal delivery.
Grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, raising oral but not IV exposure.

examples.tr: Sublingual veins drain systemically, avoiding the liver's first pass.
Too much hepatic first pass to be useful orally as an antiarrhythmic; given IV.
Deuteration slows CYP2D6 O-demethylation of the active metabolites.

lessons.title: Renal and biliary excretion

levels.kid:
After medicine does its job, the body has to throw it away. There are two main trash chutes.

The first is the **kidneys**. They are like a coffee filter. Blood goes through, and small things that dissolve in water drip out into your **pee**.

The second is **bile**. Your liver makes a green juice called bile that goes into your gut, and bigger pieces of medicine can leave the body in your **poop**.

Oily, greasy medicines are sneaky: they slip back into the blood instead of leaving. So the liver first changes them to be more watery, and then the kidneys or bile can toss them out.
levels.hs:
**Excretion** is the final removal of a drug or its metabolites from the body. The two main routes are urine (kidneys) and feces (through bile).

**Kidneys** handle drugs in three steps along the nephron:
- **Glomerular filtration**: small molecules dissolved in plasma are filtered. Drug bound to big proteins like albumin is not filtered.
- **Tubular secretion**: transporter proteins actively pump some drugs from the blood into the urine.
- **Tubular reabsorption**: as water is reabsorbed, lipophilic (fat-loving) and uncharged drugs diffuse back into the blood.

That last step explains why polar, charged drugs leave easily in urine, while lipophilic drugs need to be metabolized first into more water-soluble forms.

Urine pH matters. Making urine more alkaline traps weak acids like aspirin's salicylate in their charged form, so they cannot be reabsorbed. This is used in some poisonings.

**Biliary excretion** sends larger molecules and many metabolites (like glucuronides) from the liver into bile, then the gut. Some get "recycled": gut bacteria cut off the glucuronide and the drug is reabsorbed. This is called **enterohepatic recirculation**.
levels.college:
**Renal clearance.** CLR = (fu × GFR + CLsecretion) × (1 − Freabsorption). Filtration handles unbound drug only; albumin and large proteins are largely retained.

**Tubular secretion (proximal tubule).**
- Anions: basolateral uptake by **OAT1 and OAT3**, apical efflux by MRP2/MRP4 and others. Substrates include many penicillins, methotrexate and diuretics. Probenecid inhibits OATs, historically used to prolong penicillin exposure.
- Cations: basolateral uptake by **OCT2**, apical efflux by **MATE1 and MATE2-K**. Metformin is the classic substrate; cimetidine and dolutegravir inhibit OCT2/MATE and can raise serum creatinine without changing GFR.
- P-gp also secretes neutral and cationic drugs (digoxin).

**Passive reabsorption** depends on lipophilicity and ionization in the tubular fluid. Urine alkalinization increases excretion of weak acids with appropriate pKa (salicylate, phenobarbital); acidification would favor weak bases but is no longer used clinically.

**Biliary excretion.** Favored for higher molecular weight (roughly above 400–500 Da in humans), amphiphilic and anionic compounds and conjugates. Canalicular efflux uses MRP2, BCRP, P-gp and BSEP (bile salts). Glucuronides excreted in bile can be hydrolyzed by bacterial β-glucuronidase and the parent reabsorbed: **enterohepatic recirculation**, which produces secondary plasma peaks and prolongs half-life (mycophenolate). Irinotecan's SN-38 glucuronide is cleaved in the gut to SN-38, contributing to diarrhea.

**Chemist's rule of thumb.** Low logD (below about 0) and modest MW push toward unchanged renal clearance; lipophilic neutral compounds go hepatic; large anions often go biliary.
levels.phd:
**Physicochemical drivers.** Analyses of large datasets (Varma and colleagues; the Extended Clearance Classification System, ECCS) classify compounds by ionization, permeability and MW to predict the dominant clearance mechanism:
- Class 1A (acids/zwitterions, high permeability, MW at or below 400): metabolism.
- Class 1B (acids/zwitterions, high permeability, MW above 400): hepatic uptake (OATP).
- Class 2 (bases/neutrals, high permeability): metabolism.
- Class 3A/3B (acids/zwitterions, low permeability): renal, with hepatic uptake contributing for larger 3B compounds.
- Class 4 (bases/neutrals, low permeability): renal.
This reframes design: changing permeability or MW can switch the clearance route, not just its rate.

**Net secretion and the creatinine problem.** Creatinine is filtered and partly secreted by OCT2/MATE, so inhibitors of these transporters raise serum creatinine without true GFR loss, a frequent source of false nephrotoxicity signals in trials.

**Biliary MW thresholds** are species-dependent: rats excrete smaller molecules in bile (threshold near 325 Da) than humans (near 500 Da), so rat bile data overestimate human biliary clearance for mid-MW compounds.

**Enterohepatic recirculation kinetics** produces multiple peaks and apparent half-life prolongation; it can be interrupted by bile acid sequestrants or by antibiotics that suppress β-glucuronidase-producing bacteria, altering exposure. Inhibitors of bacterial β-glucuronidase are being studied to reduce SN-38 gut toxicity.

**Renal transporter-mediated toxicity.** OAT-dependent accumulation in proximal tubule cells underlies the nephrotoxicity of cidofovir and adefovir; coadministered probenecid reduces uptake. Aminoglycosides are taken up by megalin-mediated endocytosis. Understanding uptake versus efflux balance lets chemists predict which polar drugs concentrate in tubular cells.
levels.expert:
**What the clinic does with excretion data.** For any drug with substantial renal elimination of active parent or metabolite, regulators expect a renal impairment study, and labeling links adjustments to estimated kidney function (Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance or eGFR). A drug that is mainly metabolized but has an active, renally cleared metabolite still needs attention: the metabolite accumulates in renal failure.

**Mass balance.** A radiolabeled human ADME study (usually carbon-14) is the definitive answer to where a drug goes: percentage recovered in urine versus feces, parent versus metabolites. Fecal recovery is ambiguous: it can mean unabsorbed drug or biliary excretion, so it is interpreted with absolute bioavailability data.

**Practical pitfalls.**
- Counting only parent in urine underestimates renal handling of conjugates.
- Assuming biliary excretion is minor because a compound is small: anionic, transporter-substrate compounds can be efficiently excreted by MRP2 or BCRP regardless.
- Ignoring transporter interactions: OAT1/3, OCT2, MATE1/2-K, P-gp and BCRP are on the regulatory list of transporters to evaluate as victim and perpetrator. A secreted drug coadministered with an OAT inhibitor can show raised exposure.

**Clinical toxicology.** Urinary alkalinization is used to enhance elimination of salicylate; hemodialysis removes small, water-soluble, low-protein-binding, low-Vd toxins (lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate) effectively and is poor for highly bound or high-Vd drugs. Multiple-dose activated charcoal can interrupt enterohepatic recycling for some drugs.

**Design wisdom.** A molecule with dual clearance (part renal, part hepatic) tolerates organ impairment and interactions better. Teams sometimes tune polarity specifically to raise the renal fraction for drugs intended for patients on many CYP-interacting medicines.

keyPoints: Kidney handling = glomerular filtration + tubular secretion − reabsorption.
Only unbound drug is filtered; lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed.
OAT1/3 secrete anions; OCT2 and MATE1/2-K secrete cations.
Bile favors larger, anionic molecules and conjugates such as glucuronides.
Enterohepatic recirculation: gut bacteria cleave glucuronides and the drug is reabsorbed.

examples.tr: Probenecid blocks OAT secretion, prolonging penicillin exposure.
Ion-traps salicylate in tubular fluid, increasing excretion.
SN-38 glucuronide is cleaved by gut bacteria to SN-38, contributing to diarrhea.

lessons.title: Metabolic soft spots

levels.kid:
Some parts of a medicine are **easy to chew**. Liver enzymes are like little mouths, and they love to bite the soft parts first.

These soft parts are called **soft spots**. If an enzyme bites a soft spot, the medicine can break and may stop working, so it leaves the body too fast.

Chemists play a clever game. They find the soft spot, then put on **armor**, like swapping a hydrogen for a fluorine atom, which the enzyme can't bite. Now the medicine lasts longer!

Sometimes they do the opposite and add a soft spot on purpose, so a medicine leaves quickly when it should.
levels.hs:
A **metabolic soft spot** is a specific position on a molecule where enzymes attack most easily. Finding and fixing soft spots is one of a medicinal chemist's main jobs.

Common soft spots for **CYP450** enzymes (the liver's main oxidizers):
- Carbons next to a benzene ring (**benzylic** positions)
- Methyl groups on nitrogen or oxygen (N-methyl, O-methyl), which get removed (**dealkylation**)
- Electron-rich spots on aromatic rings, often the **para** position
- The end of long carbon chains

Other enzymes break **esters** and **amides** (hydrolysis) or attach big polar groups like glucuronic acid to **phenols** and acids.

How chemists fix soft spots:
- Put a **fluorine** or chlorine on the attacked carbon (C–F bonds are very hard to break)
- Swap a benzene for a **pyridine** ring, which is less electron-rich
- Make the molecule less greasy, since CYPs like greasy molecules
- Replace hydrogen with **deuterium**, a heavier hydrogen

Scientists find soft spots by incubating the drug with liver cells and using mass spectrometry to see which pieces gain an oxygen or lose a group.
levels.college:
**Phase I soft spots (CYP-mediated oxidation).** CYPs abstract hydrogen atoms or oxidize heteroatoms at sites that are accessible in the active site and chemically activated:
- Benzylic and allylic C–H (radical-stabilized)
- α-C–H next to N or O, leading to N- or O-dealkylation via carbinolamine or hemiacetal collapse
- Aromatic hydroxylation at electron-rich positions (para to donors), often through arene oxides
- ω and ω−1 oxidation of alkyl chains
- S-oxidation and N-oxidation (also by FMOs)
Non-CYP phase I: **aldehyde oxidase** oxidizes electron-poor azaheterocycles next to ring nitrogen; **esterases and amidases** hydrolyze esters and amides; MAO deaminates primary amines.

**Phase II soft spots.** Phenols and carboxylic acids are glucuronidated (UGTs) and sulfated (SULTs). Acyl glucuronides of carboxylic acids can be chemically reactive.

**Blocking strategies.**
- Fluorine on an aromatic para position or a benzylic site
- Replace a labile methyl with CF3, Cl, or cyclopropyl
- Introduce ring nitrogen (phenyl to pyridyl or pyrimidinyl) to lower electron density
- Steric shielding, cyclization, or conformational constraint
- Global logD reduction to lower CYP affinity
- Deuteration at rate-limiting C–H bonds

**Watch for metabolic switching**: blocking one site can redirect metabolism to the next weakest site.

**Designed soft spots.** Soft drugs such as esmolol carry esters for rapid deactivation by esterases. In celecoxib's discovery, analogs with metabolically stable substituents had extremely long half-lives in rats, so a benzylic methyl was deliberately kept as a clearance handle.
levels.phd:
**Predicting sites of metabolism (SoM).** CYP regioselectivity reflects both intrinsic reactivity (hydrogen abstraction barriers, computed by DFT or semi-empirical methods) and accessibility/orientation in the active site. Tools such as SMARTCyp combine fragment reactivity with distance-from-centroid descriptors; FAME, XenoSite and graph neural network methods learn from MetID data. Human CYP3A4's large, flexible pocket makes accessibility the weaker discriminator, while CYP2D6 favors oxidation 5–7 Å from a basic nitrogen that anchors to Asp301 and Glu216.

**Mechanistic subtleties.**
- N-dealkylation proceeds by hydrogen atom transfer (or single electron transfer for low-oxidation-potential amines), giving a carbinolamine that collapses to aldehyde and amine.
- Aromatic hydroxylation via arene oxide can show the **NIH shift** (migration of a substituent such as deuterium or a halogen).
- Fluorine blocks via C–F strength, but para-fluoro groups can be lost by ipso substitution, and fluoroalkyl groups can generate fluoroacetate-like metabolites in rare cases.

**Kinetic isotope effects** for CYP reactions are frequently masked because product release or other steps are rate-limiting, or because metabolic switching redistributes flux. Intramolecular KIE experiments reveal intrinsic isotope effects.

**Aldehyde oxidase** attacks the carbon adjacent to ring nitrogen via nucleophilic attack by the molybdenum cofactor's hydroxide; electron-poor rings are more susceptible, the opposite of CYP preferences. Blocking strategies include substitution at the reactive carbon, adding electron-donating groups, or reducing ring electron deficiency.

**Bioactivation versus clearance.** Some soft spots generate electrophiles (quinone imines from para-aminophenols, epoxides, acyl glucuronides, thiophene S-oxides). Soft spot work therefore asks two questions: how fast, and what is made.
levels.expert:
**How MetID drives the cycle.** In a typical project, a metabolically unstable lead goes into human and rat hepatocyte incubations, and high-resolution LC-MS/MS finds metabolites by mass shifts: +16 (hydroxylation or N/S-oxidation), −14 (demethylation), +176 (glucuronide), +80 (sulfate), +305 (glutathione adduct). Fragmentation localizes the site to a region, and NMR or synthetic standards confirm. The chemist then makes the minimal edit that blocks the dominant pathway and rechecks.

**Seasoned habits.**
- Fix the biggest pathway first, then recheck; metabolic switching is the rule, not the exception.
- Before blocking, ask whether lipophilicity is the true problem. A compound with logD near 4 will often find another soft spot whatever you block; lowering logD can fix clearance globally.
- Prefer edits that also help elsewhere: a pyridine nitrogen can lower logD, block oxidation and improve solubility, but may raise aldehyde oxidase risk or create new hERG or CYP-inhibition issues.
- Check human-specific pathways: aldehyde oxidase, UGT isoforms, and CYP2C19/2D6 polymorphisms.

**Polymorphism and safety.** Drugs whose clearance relies on one polymorphic enzyme show wide exposure variability. Codeine activation by CYP2D6 is a cautionary example: ultra-rapid metabolizers form more morphine, leading to regulatory restrictions in children. Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation; poor metabolizers get less benefit.

**Reactive metabolites.** Programs screen with glutathione or cyanide trapping and covalent binding studies when structural alerts (anilines, thiophenes, furans, electron-rich phenols) are present, because idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity has withdrawn drugs late. Good soft spot design aims for clean, predictable clearance to inactive, readily excreted metabolites.

keyPoints: A soft spot is the position on a molecule most easily attacked by metabolizing enzymes.
CYPs favor benzylic C–H, N/O-methyl groups, electron-rich aromatic positions and chain ends.
Blocking tools: fluorine, ring nitrogen, steric shielding, lower logD, deuteration.
Blocking one site can cause metabolic switching to another.
Soft drugs carry deliberate soft spots for rapid, predictable inactivation.

examples.tr: Lower ring electron density reduces CYP aromatic oxidation (but may invite aldehyde oxidase).
An ester soft spot is hydrolyzed by blood esterases, giving a very short action.

lessons.title: In vitro ADME assays

levels.kid:
Before a medicine is ever tried in a person, scientists test it in tiny **dishes and tubes**. It's like a practice race before the real race.

They mix the medicine with **liver cells** to see how fast it gets broken down. They put it on a layer of **gut cells** to see if it can squeeze through. They check if it sticks to **blood proteins**, and if it dissolves in water.

These quick tests are cheap and fast, so chemists can test hundreds of new molecules every week. The best ones win a ticket to the next round.
levels.hs:
**In vitro** means "in glass": experiments in test tubes, plates and cell cultures instead of living animals or people. ADME assays predict how a drug will be Absorbed, Distributed, Metabolized and Excreted.

The main ones:
- **Metabolic stability**: the drug is mixed with liver microsomes (bits of liver cells containing CYP enzymes) or whole liver cells (hepatocytes). Scientists measure how fast the drug disappears and calculate **intrinsic clearance**.
- **Permeability**: Caco-2 cells (from human colon tumor) grow as a layer like the gut wall. Scientists measure how fast the drug crosses. A simpler version, PAMPA, uses an artificial lipid membrane.
- **Solubility**: does the drug dissolve enough in water and buffers?
- **Plasma protein binding**: equilibrium dialysis measures how much drug sticks to proteins like albumin.
- **CYP inhibition**: does the drug block enzymes that other medicines need? This predicts drug interactions.
- **LogD**: how fat-loving versus water-loving the molecule is.

These tests are run in a **screening cascade**: fast, cheap tests first for many compounds, then more detailed tests for the best few before animal studies.
levels.college:
**Metabolic stability.**
- **Liver microsomes** (endoplasmic reticulum vesicles) contain CYPs, FMOs and UGTs. Incubations need NADPH; UGT activity needs UDPGA and a pore-former (alamethicin). Cytosolic enzymes (aldehyde oxidase, SULTs) are absent.
- **Hepatocytes** contain the full complement of phase I and II enzymes and transporters, making them the better predictor for diverse pathways.
- **S9 fraction** combines microsomes and cytosol.
Substrate depletion over time gives a rate constant k; CLint = k × incubation volume / amount of protein or cells, then scaled to whole liver.

**Permeability and efflux.** Caco-2 monolayers express P-gp, BCRP and other transporters; bidirectional assays give an efflux ratio (B-to-A / A-to-B Papp). A ratio above about 2 suggests active efflux, confirmed with inhibitors. MDCK-MDR1 cells are used for P-gp and CNS penetration. PAMPA measures passive diffusion only.

**Binding.** Equilibrium dialysis (or ultrafiltration, ultracentrifugation) gives fu in plasma, in brain homogenate and in microsomal incubations (fu,inc).

**Interaction assays.**
- CYP inhibition: IC50 for probe substrate metabolism (for example midazolam for CYP3A4, desipramine for CYP2D6).
- Time-dependent inhibition: IC50 shift after preincubation with NADPH, flagging mechanism-based inactivators.
- CYP induction: mRNA and activity in cultured human hepatocytes (PXR-driven CYP3A4, AhR-driven CYP1A2).
- Reaction phenotyping: recombinant CYPs and selective chemical inhibitors identify which enzyme clears the drug.

**Other.** Kinetic and thermodynamic solubility, chemical and plasma stability, logD (shake flask or chromatographic), and glutathione trapping for reactive metabolites.
levels.phd:
**IVIVE and its discontents.** Scaling CLint relies on physiological scalars (microsomal protein per gram liver, hepatocellularity, liver weight) and corrections for incubation binding and, for blood clearance, the blood-to-plasma ratio. Large analyses show systematic underprediction, commonly two- to tenfold, worse for higher clearance and for hepatocyte data. Proposed causes include loss of enzyme activity in isolated cells, unaccounted active uptake, the albumin-mediated uptake effect (protein-facilitated hepatic uptake of highly bound drugs), and model structure. Empirical "regression offsets" are widely applied.

**Low-turnover compounds.** Modern leads often show little depletion within the viability window of suspended hepatocytes. Approaches include the **hepatocyte relay method** (transfer supernatant to fresh hepatocytes repeatedly), plated hepatocytes, micropatterned cocultures (HepatoPac), and spheroids, which maintain activity over days.

**Permeability and transporters.** Apparent permeability must be interpreted with recovery (mass balance) because lipophilic compounds bind plastic and cells. Efflux ratio corrected against a transporter-knockout or inhibitor arm separates P-gp from BCRP. Uptake assays in transfected HEK293 cells (OATP1B1/1B3, OAT1/3, OCT2) feed static and PBPK interaction models.

**Regulatory framework.** ICH M12 (2024) harmonized drug interaction guidance: basic static models (R values, using unbound inhibitor concentrations) trigger clinical studies or PBPK modeling. Inhibition constants measured in vitro must account for nonspecific binding and inhibitor depletion.

**Physicochemical high-throughput.** Chromatographic logD, ChromLogD and immobilized artificial membrane retention correlate with permeability and binding; DMSO-stock kinetic solubility overestimates thermodynamic solubility for crystalline compounds because amorphous precipitates form first.
levels.expert:
**Designing a screening cascade.** A good cascade answers the program's biggest risk cheaply and early. Tier 1 (every compound): potency, logD, kinetic solubility, microsomal or hepatocyte stability in human and rat. Tier 2 (interesting compounds): permeability and efflux, plasma protein binding, CYP inhibition panel, hERG, rat PK. Tier 3 (leads): time-dependent inhibition, induction, MetID, transporter interactions, multi-species hepatocytes, reactive metabolite trapping, dog or monkey PK.

**Interpreting results like a veteran.**
- Always compare in vitro CLint predictions with in vivo rat clearance early. If they agree, trust the assay for human prediction; if rat is much higher, look for non-microsomal pathways or transporter uptake before blaming the assay.
- Low microsomal turnover with high hepatocyte turnover points to phase II, aldehyde oxidase or uptake.
- A compound "stable" in microsomes may only look stable because of high nonspecific binding; measure fu,inc.
- An efflux ratio is cell line and passage dependent; run reference compounds on every plate.
- Kinetic solubility from DMSO stocks flatters crystalline compounds; check thermodynamic solubility before formulation decisions.

**Common failures.** Over-optimizing a single metric (for example, microsomal stability) by adding lipophilic, rigid, high-binding features that then fail on solubility, hERG or free fraction. Assays are guides to a multi-parameter decision, not goals.

**Translation.** Human dose prediction combines scaled clearance, predicted Vd and target unbound concentration. Teams increasingly use PBPK models (Simcyp, GastroPlus) fed by these assays to predict human PK, food effect and interactions before first-in-human dosing, and update them as clinical data arrive.

keyPoints: In vitro = test-tube and cell assays used to predict ADME before animal or human studies.
Liver microsomes (CYPs, UGTs) and hepatocytes (full enzymes + transporters) measure metabolic stability.
Caco-2 and MDCK-MDR1 measure permeability; efflux ratio above ~2 suggests active efflux.
Equilibrium dialysis measures plasma protein binding (fu).
CYP inhibition, time-dependent inhibition and induction assays predict drug interactions.

examples.tr: CYP reactions require NADPH as a cofactor; without it, CYP turnover stops.
